title: The Enchanted Horse
paragraphs: It was the Feast of the New Year, the oldest and grandest of all the feasts in the Kingdom of Persia. The king had spent the day in the city of Schiraz, taking part in the magnificent displays his subjects had prepared in honor of the festival. The sun was going down, and the king was just about to signal his court to withdraw, when an Indian suddenly appeared before his throne. He was leading a horse in rich trappings, which looked exactly like a living one.

“Sire,” he said, bowing to the ground as he spoke, “I know I come before Your Highness very late, but I can promise you that none of the wonders you have seen today can compare with this horse, if you will only be good enough to look at him.”
“All I see,” the king replied, “is a clever copy of a real horse, and any skilled craftsman could make as much.”

“Sire,” the Indian answered, “I am not speaking of how he looks, but of what I can do with him. I need only mount him and wish myself in some particular place, and however far away it is, I will be there in a few moments. That, Sire, is what makes this horse so marvelous, and if Your Highness permits, you can test it for yourself.”

The King of Persia was fascinated by anything out of the ordinary, and he had never met a horse with such powers. He told the Indian to mount the animal and show what it could do. In an instant the man had leapt onto its back and was asking where the king wanted to send him.
“Do you see that mountain?” asked the king, pointing to a huge mass rising into the sky about three leagues from Schiraz. “Go and bring me a leaf from the palm tree that grows at its foot.”

The words had barely left the king’s mouth when the Indian turned a screw set in the horse’s neck, close to the saddle. The horse shot up into the air like lightning and was soon out of sight even of the sharpest eyes. A quarter of an hour later the Indian was seen coming back with the palm leaf in his hand. He guided his horse to the foot of the throne, dismounted, and laid the leaf before the king.
As soon as the king had seen the astonishing speed the horse was capable of, he longed to own it himself. He felt so sure the Indian would gladly sell it that he already regarded it as his.
“I never guessed from his looks how valuable an animal he was,” he told the Indian, “and I’m grateful to you for showing me my mistake. If you will sell him, name your own price.”

“Sire,” the Indian replied, “I never doubted that a ruler as wise and accomplished as Your Highness would do my horse justice once he knew its power. I even thought it likely that you would want to own it. Much as I value it, I will give it up to Your Highness on one condition. I did not build this horse myself. The man who made it gave it to me in exchange for my only daughter, who made me swear a solemn oath that I would never part with it except for something of equal value.”

“Name whatever you like,” the king cried, cutting him short. “My kingdom is large and full of fine cities. You have only to choose the one you prefer, and you shall be its ruler for the rest of your life.”

“Sire,” answered the Indian, who did not find the offer nearly as generous as the king thought it, “I am most grateful for Your Highness’s princely offer. I beg you not to be offended if I say that I can give up my horse only in exchange for the hand of the princess, your daughter.”

The courtiers burst out laughing when they heard this, and Prince Firouz Schah, the heir to the throne, was filled with anger at the Indian’s presumption. The king, however, thought it would cost him little to part with the princess in return for such a wonderful toy. While he was still hesitating over his answer, the prince broke in.
“Sire,” he said, “you cannot possibly doubt for a moment what answer to give to such an insolent bargain. Think of what you owe to yourself and to the blood of your ancestors.”

“My son,” said the king, “those are noble words, but you don’t grasp what this horse is worth. If I turn down the Indian’s proposal, he will simply make it to some other monarch, and I could not bear the thought of anyone but me owning this Seventh Wonder of the World. I am not saying I will accept his terms, and he may yet be talked into reason. In the meantime, I want you to look the horse over and, with its owner’s permission, test what it can do.”

The Indian had overheard the king, and he took it as a sign that the king was giving way. He gladly agreed to what the king wished and stepped forward to help the prince into the saddle and show him how to steer. But before he could finish, the young man turned the screw and was gone from sight.

They waited a while, expecting to see him come back across the sky at any moment. At last the Indian grew afraid. He threw himself down before the throne and said to the king, “Sire, you must have seen that the prince was too impatient to let me tell him how to return to the place he left from. I beg you not to punish me for something that was not my fault, and not to make me pay for any misfortune that may follow.”
“Then why,” cried the king, in a rush of fear and anger, “didn’t you call him back when you saw him disappear?”

“Sire,” said the Indian, “he went so fast that I was stunned, and by the time I found my voice he was already out of earshot. But let us hope he will notice a second screw and turn it, which will bring the horse back down to earth.”
“And if he does?” the king replied. “What is to stop the horse from plunging straight into the sea, or smashing him against the rocks?”
“Don’t be afraid, your Highness,” said the Indian. “This horse can cross the seas, and it will carry its rider wherever he wants to go.”

“Well, your head will answer for it,” said the monarch. “If he is not safely back with me in three months, or at least has not sent word that he is safe, you will pay with your life.” With that he ordered his guards to seize the Indian and throw him in prison.

Meanwhile Prince Firouz Schah had risen merrily into the air. For an hour he kept climbing higher and higher, until the mountains could no longer be told apart from the plains. Then he thought it was time to descend, and assumed he only had to turn the screw the opposite way. To his surprise and horror, however he turned it, it made no difference at all. Then he remembered that he had never stopped to ask how to get back to the ground, and he understood the danger he was in. Luckily he kept his head. He began going carefully over the horse’s neck, and at last, to his great joy, he found a tiny peg, much smaller than the first, close to the right ear. He turned it and felt himself sinking toward the earth, though more slowly than he had left it.

By now it was dark and the prince could see nothing, so, feeling rather uneasy, he had to let the horse choose its own course. It was past midnight when Prince Firouz Schah finally touched the ground again, faint and exhausted from the long ride and from having eaten nothing since early morning.

As soon as he dismounted, he tried to work out where he was. As far as he could tell in the thick darkness, he was standing on the terraced roof of an enormous palace, with a marble balustrade running all around it. In one corner of the terrace was a small door that opened onto a staircase leading down into the palace.

Some men would have hesitated to explore any further, but the prince did not. “I mean no harm,” he said, “and whoever owns this place will not hurt me once he sees I carry no weapon.” Afraid of putting a foot wrong, he crept carefully down the stairs. On a landing he saw an open door, and beyond it a dimly lit hall.

Before going in, the prince stopped and listened, but all he heard was the sound of men snoring. By the light of a lantern hanging from the ceiling he saw a row of black guards asleep, each with a bare sword lying beside him. He realized that this hall must be the antechamber to the rooms of some queen or princess.

Prince Firouz Schah stood perfectly still and looked around until his eyes got used to the gloom. Then he noticed a bright light shining through a curtain in one corner. He crept softly toward it, drew the folds aside, and stepped into a magnificent chamber full of sleeping women. All of them lay on low couches except one, who lay on a sofa, and he knew this must be the princess.

He stole quietly up to the side of her bed, looked at her, and saw that she was more beautiful than any woman he had ever seen. Spellbound as he was, he knew very well how dangerous his position was: a single cry of surprise would wake the guards and mean certain death for him.

So he sank softly to his knees, took hold of the princess’s sleeve, and gently drew her arm toward him. The princess opened her eyes, and at the sight of a handsome, well-dressed man in front of her she was struck speechless with astonishment.
The prince seized this moment, and bowing low as he knelt, he spoke to her like this:

“Madame, you see before you a prince in distress, the son of the King of Persia. Through an adventure so strange you will hardly believe it, I find myself here, begging for your protection. Only yesterday I was at my father’s court, taking part in the celebration of our most solemn festival. Today I am in an unknown land, with my life in danger.”

The woman whose mercy Prince Firouz Schah was asking for turned out to be the King of Bengal’s eldest daughter. She was staying for rest and a change of scene in a palace her father had built for her, not far outside the capital. She heard him out kindly and then replied:

“Prince, do not be alarmed. People in Bengal practise hospitality and kindness just as they do in Persia. Everyone here will give you the protection you ask for. You have my word on it.” The prince was about to thank her for her goodness, but she quickly went on, “As curious as I am to learn how you came here so fast, I know you must be faint with hunger. So I will tell my women to take you to one of my rooms, where you will be given supper and left to rest.”

By this time all the princess’s attendants were awake and listening to the conversation. At a sign from their mistress they got up, dressed in a hurry, and picked up some of the candles that lit the room. They led the prince to a large, high-ceilinged room, where two of them made up his bed while the rest went down to the kitchen and soon came back with every sort of dish. Then they showed him cupboards full of clothes and linen and left the room.

While they were gone, the Princess of Bengal, who had been deeply struck by the prince’s good looks, tried in vain to fall asleep again. It was no use. She was wide awake, and when her women came back in, she eagerly asked whether the prince had everything he needed, and what they thought of him.

“Madame,” they answered, “of course we cannot say what impression this young man has made on you. As for us, we think you would be lucky if the king your father let you marry someone so agreeable. There is certainly no one at the court of Bengal who can compare with him.”

The princess was far from displeased by these flattering remarks, but she did not want to give away her own feelings, so all she said was, “You are a pack of chatterboxes. Go back to bed and let me sleep.”

The next morning, as she dressed, her maids noticed that, unlike her usual self, the princess was very fussy about her appearance and had her hair done two or three times over. “For,” she said to herself, “if the prince didn’t find me unpleasant to look at when he saw me as I was, how much more will he be struck by me when he sees me in all my beauty.”

Then she put the largest and most brilliant diamonds she could find in her hair, along with a necklace, bracelets and a girdle, all made of precious stones. Her ladies laid over her shoulders a robe of the richest fabric in all the Indies, which no one but members of the royal family was allowed to wear. When she was dressed exactly as she wished, she sent to ask whether the Prince of Persia was awake and ready to receive her, since she wanted to appear before him.

When the princess’s messenger came into his room, Prince Firouz Schah was just on his way out to ask whether he might pay his respects to her mistress. But when he heard what the princess wanted, he immediately gave way. “Her wish is my law,” he said. “I am here only to obey her commands.”

A few moments later the princess herself arrived. After the usual courtesies had been exchanged, she sat down on a sofa and began to explain to the prince why she had not received him in her own apartments. “If I had,” she said, “the chief of the eunuchs could have interrupted us at any hour, since he has the right to walk in whenever he likes, whereas this place is forbidden ground to him. I am impatient to hear about the wonderful accident that has brought you here, and that is why I came to you in this room, where no one can intrude on us. So please begin, I beg you, without delay.”

So the prince began at the beginning. He told the whole story of the festival of Nedrouz, held every year in Persia, and of the splendid spectacles staged in its honor. When he came to the enchanted horse, the princess declared she could never have imagined anything half so astonishing. “Well then,” the prince went on, “you can easily see how the King my father, who loves anything out of the ordinary, was gripped by a fierce desire to own this horse, and asked the Indian what price he would take for it.

“The man’s answer was downright absurd, as you will agree when I tell you that he asked for nothing less than the hand of my sister, the princess. Everyone around us laughed and jeered, and I was beside myself with rage, but to my despair I saw that my father could not bring himself to treat the insolent demand as it deserved. I tried to argue with him, but it was no use. He only begged me to examine the horse, meaning (as I quite understood) to make me appreciate its value better.

“To please my father, I mounted the horse and, without waiting for any instructions from the Indian, turned the peg as I had seen him do. In an instant I was shooting upward, far faster than an arrow flies, and I felt I must be getting so close to the sky that I would soon knock my head against it! I could see nothing beneath me, and for a while I was so bewildered that I didn’t even know which way I was going. At last, as it was getting dark, I found another screw, and when I turned it the horse began slowly to sink toward the earth. I had to trust to chance and wait to see what fate had in store, and it was already past midnight when I found myself on the roof of this palace. I crept down the little staircase and headed straight for a light I could see through an open door—I peeped cautiously in and saw, as you can guess, the eunuchs lying asleep on the floor. I knew the risks I was running, but my need was so great that I paid them no attention, and I slipped safely past your guards to the curtain hiding your doorway.

“You know the rest, Princess. I can only thank you for your kindness and promise you my gratitude. By the law of nations I am your slave already, and the one thing I have left to give you is my heart, since that at least belongs to me. But what am I saying? Belongs to me? Alas, madame, it became yours the very moment I laid eyes on you!”
The way he spoke these words must have left the princess in no doubt about the effect of her charms, and the blush that rose to her face only made her more beautiful.

“Prince,” she replied, as soon as her confusion let her speak, “you have given me the greatest pleasure. I have followed you closely through all your adventures, and even though you are sitting right here in front of me, I trembled for your danger up in the heights of the air! Let me say how much I owe to the chance that led you to my house. You could not have entered any other that would welcome you more warmly. As for your being a slave, that is of course only a joke, and the way I received you must have shown you that you are as free here as at your father’s court. As for your heart,” she went on in an encouraging tone, “I am quite sure it was given away long ago to some princess well worthy of it, and I could not think of causing you to be unfaithful to her.”

Prince Firouz Schah was about to protest that no lady had any earlier claim on him, but one of the princess’s attendants came in just then and announced that dinner was served. When it came down to it, neither of them was sorry for the interruption.

Dinner was laid in a magnificent room, and the table was heaped with delicious fruits. During the meal, richly dressed girls sang softly and sweetly, accompanied by stringed instruments. When the prince and princess had finished, they went into a small room hung with blue and gold, which looked out on a garden planted with flowers and arbutus trees, quite unlike any found in Persia.

“Princess,” said the young man, “until now I always believed that Persia could boast finer palaces and lovelier gardens than any kingdom on earth. But my eyes have been opened, and I begin to see that wherever there is a great king, he surrounds himself with buildings worthy of him.”

“Prince,” replied the Princess of Bengal, “I have no idea what a Persian palace is like, so I can’t make comparisons. I don’t want to run down my own palace, but I assure you it is very poor beside my father the King’s, as you will agree once you have been there to greet him, which I hope you will do soon.”

The princess hoped that if she could bring the prince and her father together, the King would be so taken with the young man’s noble bearing and fine manners that he would offer him his daughter’s hand. But the Prince of Persia’s answer to her suggestion was not what she had wished for.

“Madame,” he said, “if I accept your invitation to the palace of the King of Bengal, I will satisfy my curiosity, and I will also show him the respect I feel for him. But, Princess, I think you will agree that I cannot possibly appear before so great a ruler without servants that suit my rank. He would take me for an adventurer.”

“If that is the only problem,” she replied, “you can find all the attendants you like right here. There are plenty of Persian merchants, and as for money, my treasury is always open to you. Take whatever you want.”

Prince Firouz Schah could guess what lay behind the princess’s generosity, and it touched him. But however much his love grew with every passing moment, he did not lose sight of his duty, and he answered at once:

“Princess, I cannot find words to thank you for your kind offer. I would accept it immediately, except that I keep thinking of the anxiety the King my father must be suffering because of me. I would not deserve all the love he gives me if I did not go back to him the first moment I could. While I enjoy the company of the most charming of princesses, he is, I am certain, sunk in the deepest grief, having given up every hope of seeing me again. I am sure you understand my situation. Staying away one moment longer than I must would be ungrateful of me, and perhaps even a crime, for how can I know that my absence will not break his heart?

“But,” the prince went on, “once I have done what my conscience demands, I will count the moments until, with your gracious permission, I can come before the King of Bengal, not as a wanderer but as a prince, and beg him for your hand. My father has always told me that I will be completely free in choosing a wife, and I am convinced that I need only describe your generosity for my wishes to become his.”

The Princess of Bengal was too sensible not to accept the prince’s reasons, but it troubled her greatly that he meant to leave at once. She feared that as soon as he was gone, whatever impression she had made on him would fade. So she made one more attempt to hold him. She told him she fully approved of his eagerness to see his father, and then asked him to give her just a day or two more of his company.

Out of plain courtesy the prince could hardly say no. The princess set herself to think up every kind of entertainment for him, and she did it so well that two months went by almost without his noticing, filled with balls, shows and hunting, which the princess adored as long as it was free of danger. But one day he told her gravely that he could not neglect his duty any longer, and he begged her not to put any more obstacles in his way. He promised to come back as soon as he could, with all the splendor due to her and to himself.

“Princess,” he added, “perhaps in your heart you number me among those false lovers whose devotion cannot survive being apart. If so, you do me wrong, and were I not afraid of offending you, I would beg you to come with me, because I can only be happy if my life is spent with you. As for your welcome at the Persian Court, it will be as warm as you deserve. And as for the King of Bengal, he must care far less for your happiness than you have led me to believe if he refuses to consent to our marriage.”
The princess could not find words to answer the prince’s arguments, but her silence and her lowered eyes spoke for her. They said that she had no objection to traveling with him.

The one difficulty she could think of was that Prince Firouz Schah did not know how to steer the horse, and she was afraid they might end up in the same trouble as before. But the prince calmed her fears so well that soon she thought of nothing except how to arrange their flight in such secrecy that nobody in the palace would suspect it.

They managed it. Early the next morning, while the whole palace slept, she crept up onto the roof, where the prince was already waiting with his horse’s head turned toward Persia. He mounted first and helped the princess up behind him. When she was seated firmly, with her hands gripping his belt, he turned the screw, and the horse quickly began to leave the ground below.

The horse flew at his usual speed, and Prince Firouz Schah steered him so well that after two and a half hours in the air he saw the capital of Persia spread out beneath him. He decided not to land in the great square he had set out from, nor at the Sultan’s palace, but at a country house a short distance from the town. There he showed the princess a beautiful set of rooms and asked her to rest while he told his father they had arrived and prepared a public reception worthy of her rank. Then he had a horse saddled and rode off.

All along the streets the people greeted him with cries of joy, for they had long since given up hope of seeing him again. At the palace he found the Sultan surrounded by his ministers, all dressed in the deepest mourning, and his father very nearly lost his wits for surprise and happiness at the mere sound of his son’s voice. When he had calmed down a little, he asked the prince to tell him what had happened to him.

The prince took the chance at once and told the whole story of how the Princess of Bengal had treated him, not even hiding that she had fallen in love with him. “And, Sire,” the prince finished, “I gave her my royal word that you would not refuse your consent to our marriage, and so I persuaded her to come back with me on the Indian’s horse. I left her in one of your Highness’s country houses, where she is anxiously waiting to be told that I did not promise in vain.”
At these words the prince made to throw himself at the Sultan’s feet, but his father stopped him, embraced him again, and said eagerly:

“My son, I not only consent gladly to your marriage with the Princess of Bengal, I will hurry to pay my respects to her and thank her myself for all she has done for you. Then I will bring her back with me and arrange for the wedding to be held today.”

Then the Sultan ordered the people to take off their mourning clothes, and had drums, trumpets and cymbals played together. He also commanded that the Indian be taken out of prison and brought before him.

His orders were carried out, and the Indian was brought into his presence, surrounded by guards. “I kept you locked up,” said the Sultan, “so that if my son were lost, you would pay for it with your life. Now he has come back. So take your horse and go, and never return.”

The Indian left the Sultan’s presence in haste, and once outside he asked the man who had freed him where the prince had really been all this time and what he had been doing. They told him the whole story, including that the Princess of Bengal was at that very moment waiting in the country palace for the Sultan’s consent. At once this gave the Indian an idea for taking revenge for the way he had been treated. He went straight to the country house and told the doorkeeper in charge that the Sultan and the Prince of Persia had sent him to fetch the princess on the enchanted horse and bring her to the palace.

The doorkeeper recognized the Indian and of course knew that nearly three months earlier the Sultan had thrown him into prison. Seeing him free, he assumed the man was telling the truth and had no objection to taking him to the Princess of Bengal. And the lady, hearing that he came from the prince, was glad to agree to what he asked.

Delighted that his scheme had worked, the Indian climbed onto the horse, helped the princess up behind him, and turned the peg at the very moment the prince was leaving the palace in Schiraz for the country house, with the Sultan and the whole court close behind him. The Indian knew this, and he deliberately steered the horse right over the city, so that his revenge for his unjust imprisonment would be quicker and sweeter.

When the Sultan of Persia saw the horse and its riders, he stopped dead, stunned and horrified, and burst out in oaths and curses. The Indian heard them without caring at all, knowing he was perfectly safe from pursuit. But angry and humiliated as the Sultan was, it was nothing compared to what Prince Firouz Schah felt when he saw the woman he loved so passionately carried swiftly away. He stood speechless with grief and remorse for not having guarded her better, and she vanished quickly from his sight. What was he to do? Should he follow his father into the palace and give way to despair there? His love and his courage both forbade it, and he rode on to the palace.

One look at the prince showed the doorkeeper what a foolish thing he had done, and he threw himself at his master’s feet and begged forgiveness. “Get up,” said the prince. “I am the cause of this misfortune, not you. Go and find me a dervish’s clothes, and be careful not to say they are for me.”

A short way from the country house stood a convent of dervishes, and its superior, the scheih, was a friend of the doorkeeper. So with a false story made up on the spot, it was easy to get hold of a dervish’s clothes, and the prince put them on at once in place of his own. In this disguise, with a box of pearls and diamonds hidden on him that he had meant as a gift for the princess, he left the house at nightfall. He had no idea where to go, but he was firmly resolved not to come back without her.

Meanwhile the Indian had aimed the horse in such a direction that, within a few hours, it had come down over a wood near the capital of the kingdom of Cashmere. He was very hungry, and thinking the princess might want food too, he brought his steed to the ground and left the princess in a shady spot on the bank of a clear stream.

When the princess first found herself alone, she thought of trying to run away and hide. But she had eaten hardly anything since leaving Bengal, and she felt too weak to go far, so she had to give up the idea. When the Indian came back with meats of several kinds, she ate ravenously, and soon had enough courage to answer his insolent remarks with spirit. Provoked by his threats, she leapt to her feet and screamed for help, and by good luck a band of horsemen heard her cries and rode over to ask what was wrong.

The leader of these horsemen was the Sultan of Cashmere, on his way back from the hunt. He turned at once to the Indian and asked who he was and who was with him. The Indian answered rudely that she was his wife and that nobody else had any business coming between them.

The princess, who naturally did not know the rank of the man who had come to her rescue, flatly denied the Indian’s story. “My lord,” she cried, “whoever you are, do not believe this impostor. He is a vile magician. Today he tore me away from the Prince of Persia, the man I am to marry, and brought me here on this enchanted horse.” She would have said more, but tears choked her. The Sultan of Cashmere, convinced of the truth of her story by her beauty and her noble bearing, ordered his men to cut off the Indian’s head, and it was done at once.

But although she was saved from one danger, it seemed she had only fallen into another. The Sultan ordered a horse to be given to her and led her to his own palace, where he brought her to a beautiful apartment and picked out female slaves to attend her and eunuchs to guard her. Then, without giving her time to thank him for all he had done, he told her to rest and said she should tell him her adventures the next day.

The princess fell asleep comforting herself with the thought that she had only to tell her story for the Sultan to be moved to pity and send her back to the prince without delay. But within a few hours she would learn how wrong she was.

When the King of Cashmere left her the evening before, he had made up his mind that the sun would not set again before the princess had become his wife. At daybreak his intention was announced throughout the town, to the sound of drums, trumpets, cymbals and other instruments meant to fill the heart with joy. The noise woke the Princess of Bengal early, but she did not for a moment imagine it had anything to do with her, until the Sultan came, as soon as she was dressed, to ask how she was. He told her that the blasts of the trumpets she heard were part of the solemn marriage ceremonies, and begged her to get ready. This unexpected news filled the princess with such terror that she sank to the floor in a dead faint.

The slaves who were waiting on her ran to help, and the Sultan himself did his best to bring her round, but for a long while it was all useless. At last her senses slowly began to return, and then, rather than break faith with the Prince of Persia by agreeing to such a marriage, she decided to pretend to be mad. She began by saying all kinds of nonsense and making strange gestures, while the Sultan stood watching her with sorrow and surprise. But since this sudden fit showed no sign of passing, he left her with her women and ordered them to take the greatest care of her. Still, as the day went on, the illness seemed to grow worse, and by night it was almost violent.

Days went by like this, until the Sultan of Cashmere finally decided to call all the doctors of his court together to discuss her sad condition. They answered that madness comes in so many different kinds that it was impossible to give an opinion without seeing the princess. So the Sultan ordered that they be brought into her chamber one at a time, each according to his rank.

The princess had foreseen this. She knew that if she once let the physicians take her pulse, even the dimmest of them would see she was perfectly healthy and that her madness was an act. So whenever one came near, she flew into such violent fits that none of them dared lay a finger on her. A few who wanted to seem wiser than the rest announced that they could judge a patient by sight alone, and prescribed her various potions. She took these without any fuss, since she was sure they could do her no harm.

When the Sultan of Cashmere saw that his court doctors could do nothing to cure the princess, he summoned the doctors of the city, and they fared no better. Next he sent for the most famous physicians of the other large towns. When their learning proved unequal to the task as well, he finally dispatched messengers to the neighboring states, carrying a written account of every detail of the princess’s madness. He promised to pay the expenses of any physician who came to see her for himself, and a generous reward to whoever cured her. Many foreign scholars answered this call and crowded into Cashmere, but of course they succeeded no better than the others, because the cure depended not on them or their skill but only on the princess herself.

Meanwhile Prince Firouz Schah had been roaming from place to place, sad and without hope. During this time he reached a large city in India, where he heard people talking at length about the Princess of Bengal, who had lost her senses on the very day she was to marry the Sultan of Cashmere. That was reason enough for him to set out for Cashmere. At the first inn where he stayed in the capital, he asked for the whole story. When he learned that he had found the princess he had lost so long ago, he began working out a plan to rescue her.

First he got himself a doctor’s robe. Together with the long beard he had grown on his travels, it would leave no doubt about his profession. Then he went straight to the palace and was received by the chief usher. He apologized for his boldness in thinking he could cure the princess when so many others had failed, but he said he knew the secret of certain remedies that had never yet failed to work.
The chief usher told him he was most welcome, and that the Sultan would be glad to receive him. If he succeeded, he would earn a magnificent reward.

When the Prince of Persia was brought before him in his physician’s disguise, the Sultan did not waste words. He only remarked that the mere sight of a doctor sent the princess into fits of rage. Then he took the prince up to a room under the roof. It had an opening from which he could watch the princess without being seen himself.

The prince looked through it and saw the princess lying on a sofa with tears in her eyes. She was softly singing to herself a song that mourned her sad fate, which had taken from her, perhaps for ever, the one she loved so dearly. The young man’s heart pounded as he listened. He needed no more proof that her madness was pretended, and that it was love for him that had made her turn to this kind of trick. He quietly left his hiding place and went back to the Sultan. He told him that certain signs convinced him her illness was not incurable, but that he would have to see her and speak with her alone.

The Sultan raised no objection and ordered that he be shown into the princess’s apartment. The moment she saw his physician’s robe, she leapt up from her seat in a fury and hurled insults at him. The prince paid no attention to her behavior. He came right up to her, so that only she could hear, and whispered, “Look at me, princess, and you will see that I am no doctor. I am the Prince of Persia, and I have come to set you free.”

At the sound of his voice the Princess of Bengal grew calm all at once, and her face filled with joy, the kind that comes only when the thing we want most and expect least suddenly happens. For a while she was too overwhelmed to speak. Prince Firouz Schah used her silence to tell her everything that had happened: his despair at seeing her vanish before his eyes, the oath he had sworn to follow her across the world, and his delight at finally finding her in the palace at Cashmere. When he had finished, he asked her in turn to tell him how she had come to be there, so that he could better work out a way to rescue her from the Sultan’s tyranny.

A few words from the princess were enough to explain the whole situation. She had been forced to play the madwoman to escape marrying the Sultan, who had not even been polite enough to ask for her consent. If it came to that, she added, she had made up her mind to die rather than be forced into such a marriage and break faith with a prince she loved.

The prince then asked whether she knew what had become of the enchanted horse since the Indian’s death. The princess could only say she had heard nothing about it. Still, she did not think the Sultan could have forgotten it, after all she had told him about its value.

The prince agreed, and the two of them talked over a plan by which she could escape and go back with him to Persia. As a first step, she was to dress with care and receive the Sultan politely when he visited her the next morning.

When the Sultan heard how the interview had gone, he was overjoyed. His opinion of the doctor’s skill rose higher still the next day, when the princess treated him so graciously that he was convinced her cure would not be long in coming. All the same, he held back and merely told her how glad he was to see her so much better. He urged her to make full use of such a clever physician and to trust him completely. Then he left, without waiting for any reply from the princess.

The Prince of Persia left the room with him and humbly asked whether he might inquire how the Princess of Bengal had come to Cashmere, so far from her father’s kingdom, and why she had been alone. The Sultan thought this a natural question and told him the same story the princess had told. He added that he had ordered the enchanted horse taken to his treasury as a curiosity, though he had no idea how it was used.

“Sire,” replied the physician, “your Highness’s account has given me the clue I needed to finish the princess’s recovery. On her journey here on an enchanted horse, some of its enchantment must have passed into her own body, and only certain perfumes, whose secret I hold, can drive it out. If your Highness is willing to give the court and the people one of the most astonishing sights they have ever seen, order the horse brought into the great square outside the palace, and leave the rest to me. I promise that within a few moments, before the whole assembled crowd, you will see the princess as healthy in mind and body as she has ever been in her life. And to make the sight as impressive as possible, I suggest she be richly dressed and covered in the finest jewels of the crown.”

The Sultan gladly agreed to everything the prince proposed. The next morning he had the enchanted horse taken from the treasury and brought into the great square of the palace. Word soon spread through the town that something extraordinary was about to happen. So many people gathered that the guards had to be called out to keep order and clear a path for the enchanted horse.

When everything was ready, the Sultan appeared and took his seat on a platform, with the chief nobles and officers of his court around him. Once they were seated, the Princess of Bengal was seen coming out of the palace with the ladies the Sultan had assigned to her. She walked slowly up to the enchanted horse and, with her ladies’ help, climbed onto its back. As soon as she was in the saddle, with her feet in the stirrups and the bridle in her hand, the physician set some large braziers full of burning coals around the horse. Into each he threw a perfume made of all kinds of sweet scents. Then he folded his hands across his chest and, with eyes lowered, walked three times around the horse, muttering certain words as he went. Soon a thick smoke rose from the braziers and almost hid the horse and the princess. This was the moment he had been waiting for. He sprang lightly up behind the lady, leaned forward and turned the peg. As the horse shot up into the air, he called out so that everyone present could hear, “Sultan of Cashmere, when you want to marry princesses who have come to you for protection, first learn to win their consent.”

That was how the Prince of Persia rescued the Princess of Bengal and brought her back to Persia. This time they landed in front of the King’s own palace. The wedding was put off only as long as it took to make the ceremony as splendid as possible. As soon as the celebrations were over, an ambassador was sent to the King of Bengal to tell him what had happened and to ask his approval of the alliance between the two countries, which he gave gladly.
